cards.explanation: The answer is wail, friends. Isaiah opens with “Wail, O ships of Tarshish…” (Isaiah 23:1). The news is so heavy that even the ships get told to cry out. I think that's about the saddest way you could start a message.

The ships of Tarshish should wail because Tyre is laid waste, “…without house or harbor.” Ships sail toward a port, so I think a city with no harbor left is news that hits them hard. That's a lot of loss packed into one verse, friends.

The answer is True, friends. The verse says word has reached them from the land of Cyprus. So the news about Tyre comes to the ships of Tarshish from Cyprus. That's a detail that's easy to slide past.

The answer is True. Isaiah says, “Be silent, O dwellers of the coastland, you merchants of Sidon…” (Isaiah 23:2). These are traders who spent their days making deals and crossing the sea. Now they're told to hush. I'd bet that's the quietest that coast ever got.

The answer is merchant, friends. Isaiah says Tyre “…was the merchant of the nations.” (Isaiah 23:3). Grain from the Nile came across the water, and its harvest was Tyre's revenue. Merchant is the title the verse gives her.

The answer is ashamed, friends. Isaiah says, “Be ashamed, O Sidon, the stronghold of the sea…” (Isaiah 23:4). A stronghold is supposed to be a place that holds up. Tyre has been laid waste, and Sidon gets this message right after.

The answer is that they will writhe in agony. Isaiah says, “When the report reaches Egypt, they will writhe in agony over the news of Tyre.” (Isaiah 23:5). That's a strong word for their reaction, friends. Egypt is also the land of the Nile harvest that Isaiah just said was Tyre's revenue (Isaiah 23:3).
The answer is False, friends. Isaiah says Tyre's “…origin is from antiquity…” (Isaiah 23:7). She's an ancient city, and her feet have taken her to settle far away. Old city, long reach.
The answer is the LORD of Hosts. Isaiah says, “The LORD of Hosts planned it…” (Isaiah 23:9). Isaiah asks who planned it, and then he answers his own question. Plain and direct, friends.

The answer is to disgrace all the renowned of the earth. The LORD of Hosts planned it “…to disgrace all the renowned of the earth.” The verse also says it was to defile all of Tyre's glorious beauty. Tyre had a famous name, and the verse goes straight at it, friends.

The answer is that there is no longer a harbor, and the verse says it plainly: “there is no longer a harbor.” (Isaiah 23:10). That's why the Daughter of Tarshish is told to cultivate her land like the Nile. The harbor is the reason Isaiah gives. That's the whole answer, friends.

The answer is destroyed, friends. The LORD “…has given a command that the strongholds of Canaan be destroyed.” (Isaiah 23:11). That's a big verse, because His hand is stretched out over the sea and kingdoms tremble. Heavy words.

The answer is no place of rest. The LORD says, “…even there you will find no rest.” Cyprus looks like the next stop on the map. But the Virgin Daughter of Sidon is told there is no rest there either. I think that's one of the hardest lines in the chapter, friends.

The answer is True, friends. Isaiah says of the land of the Chaldeans that “The Assyrians destined it for the desert creatures…” (Isaiah 23:13). They set up their siege towers, stripped its palaces and brought it to ruin. Isaiah points at that land as something to look at.
The answer is seventy, friends. Isaiah says, “…Tyre will be forgotten for seventy years…” (Isaiah 23:15). Then he ties the number to the span of a king's life. That's a long stretch to be forgotten.

The answer is so she will be remembered. That's the reason in the song: “Make sweet melody, sing many a song, so you will be remembered.” She's called a forgotten harlot, so the harp and the songs are meant to bring her back to people's minds. That's all the song gives as the reason, friends.

The answer is False, friends. Isaiah says, “…at the end of seventy years, the LORD will restore Tyre.” (Isaiah 23:17). The seventy years of being forgotten come to an end. That's the turn in the verse.

The answer is False, friends. Isaiah says her profits and wages will be set apart to the LORD, and they “…will not be stored or saved…” Tyre was a city that lived on revenue, so this is a big change. The money has a different destination.

The answer is abundant food and fine clothing. Tyre's profit goes to those who live before the LORD, “…for abundant food and fine clothing.” That's the last verse of the chapter, and it lands somewhere nobody would've guessed. Plenty to eat and good things to wear, friends.
